result.summary: Do not dispatch yet: the act-time absence exception can still leave registered jobs pointing at a deleted core.

findings.title: A vanished schedule file does not prove its registration disappeared
findings.body: D6 drops a disclosed candidate on ENOENT/ENOTDIR and continues teardown. Consider an unrecorded wienerdog-dream.xml deleted during the confirmation prompt: the manifest comparison still passes, but the registered Windows task survives because registration stores its command in Task Scheduler's database (src/cli/schedule.js). D5a skips its unload, no manifest entry provides another attempt, and uninstall deletes the core around the registered task. This recreates the orphan being closed; R-failed-unload does not cover it because no unload was attempted.
findings.recommendation: Distinguish absence during initial discovery from disappearance of an already-disclosed unloadable candidate. Require the latter to stop core teardown with recovery metadata retained. Add a regression where discovery succeeds, the XML disappears before D5a, and its registered task remains.

next_steps: Revise D6, D15 and the act-time acceptance criteria to cover disappearance after disclosure.
